description: Electronics Engineering student (UNAL, Colombia). My idea for this track: derive CO2, CO and H2O production rates of comets directly from SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (spectral WCS, static-sky subtraction, band fitting, Haser model) and publish them in an interactive web app. Looking for strong technical profiles: scientific Python (astropy/numpy), signal processing or statistics, astronomy/physics, and frontend (React/TypeScript, WebGL/D3). Rigor first.
summary: Breathing Comets is a public, open-source web instrument that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky spectral survey into a time machine for the changing infrared sky. Enter any name or RA/Dec and it streams real north-up SPHEREx Level-2 cutouts (DR1+QR3, l2b-v27) as a dated sequence: play them, blink two epochs, or use Diff λ, a wavelength-matched difference that subtracts a static-sky reference built from other visits at the same filter wavelength, so moving and variable sources stand out instead of filter residue. Any pixel yields a forced-ePSF spectrum over 0.75–5.0 µm; band medians on 41 stars agree with 2MASS/WISE within ±3%. The five challenge targets are prepared and verified: Barnard's Star moves 10.6 ± 0.4″/yr (Gaia DR3: 10.39″/yr); ε Indi B parallax is 271 ± 20 mas (Gaia: 270.7 mas); WISE 0855's synthetic W2 is 0.45 ± 0.02 (stat.) mJy (published: 0.48 mJy). Beyond the brief, a comet atlas measures CO₂ production for 20 comets with a ν₃ band model and Haser Monte Carlo (3I/ATLAS: 1.17×10²⁷ s⁻¹, inside the published range), and a Small-Body Lab gives NEATM diameters for 28 near-Earth asteroids, with a retained cross-validation diagnostic against 50 NEOWISE objects (−33%/+36%; blind re-validation pending). Every number keeps its interval, provenance and limits; nothing is simulated. Views are shareable by URL, bilingual (EN/ES), mobile-ready and GPL-3.0, so anyone can see, and check, how the sky changes.
details:
Breathing Comets: see, measure and verify how the infrared sky changes

Live product: https://breathingcomets.org · Method and limits: https://breathingcomets.org/method · Source code (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/sebastianvelace/Breathing-Comets

1. The problem

The Planet X and SPHEREx challenge asks for a public web tool that displays SPHEREx images and makes it easy for anyone to see how they change over time. Pluto was found by blinking two photographic plates of the same sky. SPHEREx now images the whole sky in 102 infrared channels every six months, but its Level-2 products are 2040 × 2040 FITS frames in a public S3 bucket. In those frames every detector row sees a different wavelength through a linear variable filter (LVF), so a naive difference of two visits leaves a residue on almost every star. Breathing Comets removes those barriers without hiding the physics: it is a browser instrument for time-domain inspection, built on real mission files and quantitatively checked against independent catalogues.

2. What it does

  • Search and stream. Enter a prepared target, a stellar name or sexagesimal/decimal RA/Dec. The tool resolves the position, finds every covering exposure in an index of 809,593 exposures (detectors D4–D6; 1,630,148 S3 keys), reprojects north-up cutouts and streams them by date. Each frame keeps its detector, central wavelength, UTC date, MJD, observation ID and provenance.
  • Play, blink, compare. Exposures play as a short movie at a fixed brightness scale (asinh stretch, 0.5–99.5% clip) so that brightness changes are real, not re-stretched. A two-date comparison blinks the first and last useful visits.
  • Diff λ (wavelength-matched difference). For each frame, a static-sky reference is built from up to 8 frames of other visits whose wavelength lies within 3 channel widths. Reference pixels in the official hard-mask categories are discarded before fitting. Per pixel, a 3σ-clipped linear fit in wavelength is used when the usable references bracket the frame's wavelength; otherwise their median is used (no extrapolation), and those pixels carry a DIFF_MEDIAN_FALLBACK flag because that fallback is a colour-dependent approximation. A pixel needs at least 3 usable references, otherwise it is reported unavailable. The difference uses a ±5σ display scale, with σ = 1.4826 × MAD: a moving source appears positive where it is and negative where it was. That scale is not a calibrated temporal significance.
  • Gaia overlay. Gaia DR3 positions are propagated with their proper motions to the epoch of each displayed frame and shifted for SPHEREx's observer parallax, so the expected position moves with the movie. Against an Astropy/DE440 geocentric reference the marker agrees within 5 mas (it was up to 0.53″ before parallax was applied); for Barnard's Star the parallax shift is 0.3–0.5″.
  • One-click spectrum. Clicking any sky position runs forced photometry with the exposure's sampled effective PSF (radius 4 px, free background) in every covering exposure and plots flux versus wavelength, with molecular and hydrogen line markers (Paβ, Paα, Brα, H₂O, CH₄, CO₂ ν₃, CO 1–0).
  • Lab mode. A pixel and quality-flag inspector, links to the original FITS files, a data-cube view, and an Aladin Lite reference viewer with the SPHEREx DR1 spectral cube (HiPS), Gaia and 2MASS layers.
  • Share and embed. Every view (target, detector, channel, epochs, mode, stretch, layers, language) is encoded in the URL; an embed route serves the same view. Interface in English and Spanish.

3. Results on the five challenge targets

  • Barnard's Star: SPHEREx proper motion 10.6 ± 0.4″/yr against Gaia DR3 10.39″/yr (formal error ±0.10″/yr; ±0.4 includes frame systematics from a saturated core and 3 useful visits). Parallax is reported as not measurable because the core is saturated.
  • ε Indi B: proper motion 4.75 ± 0.04″/yr (Gaia DR3 4.68″/yr). Differential parallax against 4 Gaia field stars: 271 ± 20 mas, against Gaia DR3 270.7 mas (ε Ind A: 274.8 mas). The error comes from a per-visit bootstrap over 9 visits; dropping one control star gives 277–294 mas, and we show that sensitivity.
  • WISE 0855−0714 (the coldest known brown dwarf): below 3.8 µm the flux is ≈ 0 once it is deblended from a Gaia star 6.8″ away (J ≈ 25). A synthetic W2 through the real W2 response gives 0.45 ± 0.02 mJy, against published W2 ≈ 0.48 mJy and CatWISE2020 0.51 mJy. The ±0.02 mJy is statistical and conditional on how the 14% of the W2 response beyond SPHEREx's 5.0 µm limit is filled (a flat extension of the 4.97 µm bin). Setting that tail to zero or doubling it gives 0.41–0.49 mJy; no WISE colour correction is applied, and the AllWISE value is blended at the 2010 position.
  • R Draconis (Mira): variability timescale ≈ 229 d (225–241) at 3.8–5.0 µm against a catalogued 245.6 d. The peak-to-peak range falls from 2.0 mag at 0.9 µm to 0.7 mag at 4.4 µm. Only 1.9 cycles are covered, so this is presented as consistent with the catalogue, not as an independent period.
  • RW Aurigae (young star): from 2025-09 to 2026-09 the optical flux rose ×1.8 while 4–5 µm fell ×0.5. This anti-correlation is consistent with inner-disk hot dust; only three epochs are available, and the page says so.

4. Beyond the brief: what comets exhale and how big asteroids are

SPHEREx is uniquely sensitive to H₂O, CO₂ and CO, which is exactly what comets release. We built two science modules on the same data path.

  • Comet atlas (20 comets). Sky-subtracted spectra are fitted with a physical CO₂ ν₃ band model (P and R branches, even rotational levels, rotational temperature and a free wavelength shift) in D5 (3.85–4.42 µm). CO is fitted in D6 (4.60–4.74 µm) and H₂O in D4 (2.50–2.86 µm). Production rates come from a Haser parent model in a 3 px aperture with a 40–55 px background ring, using fluorescence g-factors at 1 au of 2.86×10⁻³ s⁻¹ (CO₂), 2.46×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (CO) and 4.24×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (H₂O). Uncertainties come from a 4,000-draw Monte Carlo over flux, 5% calibration, 5% g-factor, lognormal lifetime (0.3) and lognormal outflow speed (0.2), reported as 16/50/84 percentiles. A detection requires S/N ≥ 5 and χ²ᵣ < 50; S/N ≥ 5 with χ²ᵣ ≥ 50 is labelled "with systematics", and 3 ≤ S/N < 5 "marginal". Current status: 17 detected, 2 with systematics, 1 marginal, 0 not detected. A detection means a significant band excess, not by itself a well-constrained Q: two detections with no channel in the band core (235P/LINEAR, C/2025 Q3) are flagged as weakly constrained, because a retained injection test recovered 0.32–5.0 × the injected flux in that regime. On 79 null apertures the rule gave 0 false positives (retained research notes; not a Gaussian false-alarm probability). The channel response is approximated by a Gaussian rather than the released transmission profiles, so the errors are conditional on that profile. The outflow speed is v = v₀ r_h^−0.5 km/s with v₀ = 0.85; the alternative v₀ = 0.50 lowers Q by about 40%.
  • Consistency with the literature. For 3I/ATLAS in August 2025, Q(CO₂) = 1.17×10²⁷ s⁻¹ lies inside the published 9.4×10²⁶–1.6×10²⁷ s⁻¹ range (Lisse et al. 2025; Lisse et al. 2026). For 29P/Schwassmann–Wachmann in December 2025, Q(CO) = 4.5×10²⁸ s⁻¹ lies inside the published 2.9–5.6×10²⁸ s⁻¹ range (Bockelée-Morvan et al. 2022), with CO/CO₂ = 43.8 [36.6–51.9]. These are labelled consistency checks, not independent confirmations: the 3I range is the envelope of a preliminary and an updated estimate from the same campaign (updated: 1.6×10²⁷ s⁻¹ ± 10%), under assumptions that are not yet harmonised with ours. Our August value agrees with the preliminary estimate and lies below the updated one: our 16–84% upper bound is 1.38×10²⁷ s⁻¹. An unsupported H₂O comparison for 3I/ATLAS is withheld rather than shown.

. An unsupported H₂O comparison for 3I/ATLAS is withheld rather than shown.

  • Small-Body Lab (near-Earth asteroids). Thermal diameters use NEATM plus reflected light (HG, G = 0.15; ε = 0.9) with beaming parameter η = 1.48 ± 0.44, using only trails ≤ 3 px. A retained cross-validation against 50 NEOWISE objects gives a SPHEREx/NEOWISE ratio of 0.67–1.36 (16–84%), about −33%/+36%. We present it as a diagnostic, not a validated error distribution: η was held out per object, but each held-out thermal template still used that object's NEOWISE diameter and albedo, which the estimator for new objects cannot use. A blind re-validation with the production estimator is the next step. The median of 1.02 is 1 by construction because η is fitted, and we state that it is not an accuracy figure. From 86 candidates we publish 11 tier-A and 17 tier-B diameters, including 7 potentially hazardous asteroids, plus 6 explicitly provisional entries. Each carries its 16–84% interval, evidence tier, a ±35% systematic floor and single-visit warnings. "PHA" is shown as an orbit class, not an impact prediction.

5. How it works (architecture and calibration)

  • Data path. A Python/FastAPI service reads SPHEREx L2 files directly from NASA/IRSA's public S3 bucket and reads their FITS layout without downloading whole files. It assigns each pixel its wavelength from the full-resolution spectral WCS (cal-swcs-v5-2026-191), never subsampled: 4× subsampling keeps the 99th percentile within 1 nm but hides jumps of hundreds of nanometres at detector edges. Pixels within 20 px of an edge are excluded from spectra. Cutouts are reprojected north-up with Astropy/reproject and packed into a compact binary stack format (SPXF). 38 stacks are precomputed so that the challenge targets and tracked comets load instantly even if the live API is unavailable. Comets are tracked with JPL Horizons ephemerides computed for SPHEREx as the observer.
  • Calibration choices. The official quality mask rejects SUR_ERROR, NONFUNC, DICHROIC, MISSING_DATA, HOT, COLD, NONLINEAR, PERSIST, BLOOM, SNOWBALL, HALO and SATELLITE_HALO. Saturated (OVERFLOW) pixels are flagged rather than masked, following the SPHEREx team's recommendation. No aperture correction is applied, because the SPHEREx absolute gain is ePSF-based; an early version that applied one counted the PSF wings twice and put W2 10% high. Each point carries a 3% flux systematic in quadrature. The v5 spectral calibration shifts D5/D6 by +6.3 nm, in the same direction as the 3.7 ± 0.9 nm CO₂-band offset our comet census had measured independently; band shifts remain free in every fit.
  • Photometric validation. On 41 isolated stars in the CDFS, COSMOS and NEP fields, the SPHEREx/catalogue flux ratios are J 0.982 ± 0.020, H 1.008 ± 0.038, Ks 1.011 ± 0.033, W1 0.972 ± 0.014 and W2 0.996 ± 0.014 (mean 0.994). These are band medians with robust (MAD-based) scatter for a selected sample, from a power law evaluated at the isophotal wavelength, so they support the flux scale to about ±3%. They do not establish ±3% per source (the ordinary J standard deviation is 8.35%), and they are not response-convolved synthetic photometry.
  • Front end. A static SvelteKit/TypeScript application on Cloudflare Pages decodes stacks in a Web Worker and uploads frames progressively to a WebGL2 renderer, which shades blink and difference modes on the GPU. Charts use uPlot. Aladin Lite is loaded only in Lab mode. The API runs on Fly.io with a persistent cache.
  • Resampling and variance. Cutouts use bilinear resampling. Each output pixel inherits the flags of every contributing native pixel, and variance is propagated as Σ wᵢ² Var(xᵢ); covariance between neighbouring output pixels is not represented.
  • Scientific audit. On 15 November 2026 a line-by-line audit of the FITS access, masks, reprojection, Diff λ, photometry and comet and asteroid models reported 2 high- and 9 medium-priority findings. We fixed the two code defects with regression tests (hard-flagged references could leak into Diff λ; resampled variance used linear rather than squared weights) and rebuilt the five prepared difference packages. The audit's own probe now reports zero residual effect. Claims it showed to be overstated (asteroid CV, W2 error, ±3% scope, outflow law, zero-core comets) are now scoped in the product. The report and its reproducible probes are in the repository.
  • Verification. Unit, contract, numerical, browser (Playwright) and deployment checks run against real data. The /method page is generated from the same data files the product uses and records the data release, the spectral WCS version and the build commit.
  • On the deployed site, 73 automated browser tests pass, covering real API spectra, all five targets with the API blocked, shared URLs, both languages, phones and the legal pages.

6. Benefits and impact

  • For the public and educators: the classic blink comparison now works on a modern, 102-colour infrared survey from any phone or laptop, with no installation, account or FITS knowledge.
  • For citizen scientists and students: shareable, reproducible views make it possible to discuss one exact frame, epoch and pixel. Every number links to its method and caveats.
  • For researchers: quick-look time-domain and spectral inspection of any SPHEREx field, downloadable stacks (SPXF) and JSON data, a public comet CO₂ census, and NEO sizes with honest intervals. The tool is a triage layer, not a replacement for a full pipeline.
  • Scientific integrity as a feature: nothing is simulated. Missing coverage, saturated cores, blended photometry and unverified comparisons are shown as such instead of being filled in.
  • Open and safe by design: plain-language Terms of use and Privacy notice (EN/ES) at breathingcomets.org/terms and /privacy. No accounts, cookies or analytics, and no agency logos.

7. What we hope to achieve

We want SPHEREx's time domain to be as approachable as Pluto's discovery plates. Next steps are a published injection–recovery test for the comet pipeline (until then we claim no completeness or false-alarm rate), automatic moving-object candidates from Diff λ residuals cross-matched with JPL small-body identification, and continuous updates as new SPHEREx releases arrive.

8. Known limits (stated in the product)

  • The comet atlas is a census by pass, not a real-time monitor: objects are revisited a few times a year and public data lag by weeks.
  • Gas band flux scales as Q r_h⁻² Δ⁻², so Q is not trusted beyond about 10 au.
  • A field requested for the first time takes about 5–20 s to stack (measured 2–22 s, depending on coverage and catalogue services); repeat views and the five precomputed targets load instantly. Coverage differs by detector.
  • Moving objects are not tracked inside the Explorer: searching a comet or asteroid explains this and links to its tracked comet page (29P, 3I/ATLAS), the comet atlas or the Small-Body Lab.
  • The viewer requires a WebGL2-capable browser with hardware acceleration enabled.
  • Some headline results are retained research summaries whose generators are not yet public (asteroid NEATM fits and CV, ε Indi B parallax, comet band-fit intervals, null and injection tests); the method page labels them.
  • A professional multi-comet catalogue exists (68 comets, results not public). We do not claim a first census; our contribution is a public, reproducible tool with its checks.

9. Tools, languages and software

TypeScript, Svelte/SvelteKit, Vite, WebGL2 (twgl.js), uPlot, Aladin Lite 3.8.2, Comlink, fflate, TanStack Query, Paraglide (i18n), Bits UI, GSAP, Lenis, Geist and Geist Mono fonts (SIL OFL 1.1). Python with FastAPI, Granian, Astropy, astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, DuckDB, PyArrow, obstore, cdshealpix, httpx and Pydantic. Tests with pytest, Vitest and Playwright. Hosting on Cloudflare Pages (web) and Fly.io (API). Demo video built with HyperFrames (HTML-to-video), Kokoro TTS and MusicGen.

10. Use of AI (transparency)

AI coding assistants (Claude Code with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2; Codex with GPT Astra 6) were used for software implementation, debugging, tests and documentation, under the team's direction and review. The demo video's narration (Kokoro TTS) and background music (MusicGen) are AI-generated. The video carries a visible on-screen AI watermark and end-card credits, and its file metadata declares AI generation. All scientific sky images are real SPHEREx observations; no image, spectrum or measurement is AI-generated. Every scientific statement is tied to retained measurements, catalogue values or cited publications, and was checked numerically. The decorative starfield background of the interface is not data and is kept separate from the scientific plates.
